strategy.title: Four signed holiday delivery blocks, run by Petal Route Couriers
strategy.why: Four shop owners signed $1,800 block orders in writing; Petal Route Couriers LLC confirmed in writing it can run all 400 deliveries days 7-21 at $1,100 a block, invoiced net 30. $7,200 settles by day 24 of 35 (even three blocks, $5,400, clear the $4,000 target). The courier is paid from receipts, so no capital is advanced. The work is the courier's, not the owner's: Brain's physical-work exclusion overlooks the named subcontractor.

reviews.reasons: EXECUTABLE is right, and the disagreement with Brain's exclusion is correct. Brain excluded cop_20b433d2bef04525aa92 because 'nothing names an independent supplier or subcontractor', but the card's fulfillmentOwner and its EVIDENCE fulfillment fact name Petal Route Couriers LLC, which quoted $1,100 a block net 30 and confirmed in writing it can run all 400 deliveries days 7-21 (up to 40/day). The courier, the recorded fulfiller, performs the physical work, not the owner. Every link is established on the record: four WRITTEN_ACCEPTANCE agreements at $1,800 each (a real price these buyers signed, not a benchmark), so conversion and volume are the four signed buyers themselves; fulfilment capacity 15 days x 40 = 600 >= 400 deliveries; each shop pays within 3 days of its block's last delivery (day 21), clearing by day 24 of 35. Arithmetic recomputed: 4 x $1,800 = $7,200 settled by day 24 >= $4,000; three blocks ($5,400) would still clear it. Courier cost 4 x $1,100 = $4,400 is invoiced net 30 and falls due about day 51, paid from receipts, so no capital is advanced and pre-proof spend is $0. The excluded window-display opening is correctly rejected: $250 is only the owner's word (PERSON), and 85 shops x 9/40 = ~19 at most, 17 needed even at that unproven price.
findings: The target is met as gross settled cash, which is the contract's metric; the owner's net from the plan is $7,200 - $4,400 = $2,800, and a $4,400 courier payable is outstanding at day 35. Booking the courier on day 1 is a commitment owed even if a shop defaults; the four signed orders back it, but the owner should know the obligation precedes the receipts.
If any shop pays late or disputes, three paid blocks still reach $5,400, so a single default does not break the target.
